Air Quality Around the Ports

Understanding fine-particle and black-carbon pollution patterns near the Ports of Los Angeles and Long Beach.

Where
Los Angeles & Long Beach, California
Period
2019–2025
Go to the charts

Dashboard and Purpose

The Ports of Los Angeles and Long Beach are two of the busiest container ports in the country, and the trucks, trains, ships, and equipment that keep them running are concentrated in and around a handful of Southern California neighborhoods. This dashboard looks at what air-quality monitors near both ports have recorded over the past several years, including the fine particle pollution (PM2.5) and black carbon (soot) and lays out the patterns in plain terms: how they've changed year to year, when they spike, how often they cross federal health thresholds, and how they vary by time of day and by location. It is important to note that where a chart shows a spike, gap, or gradient, the text around it says what the data indicates and suggests, not what it definitively proves. Some spikes in this dataset (wildfire smoke, fireworks holidays) come from sources unrelated to port activity and the charts and captions call those out where relevant.

This dashboard focuses on air-quality monitoring data. Its companion, the Gate Move Activity Dashboard, focuses on port truck activity. Viewed together, the two help build a fuller picture of the relationship between port operations and the air quality experienced by nearby communities, without assuming a conclusion the data alone can't support. They should not be interpreted as direct measures of individual health risk.

Looking for port activity data? Truck gate-move volumes, monthly trends, and COVID-19 impact analysis for both ports live in the separate Gate Move Activity Dashboard which serves as the dashboard's companion piece.

 

Understanding the Data

This dashboard shows patterns and comparisons in monitoring data. It does not, on its own, prove that port operations caused any specific pollution level or health outcome.

  1. 1

    Port Activity

    Trucks, trains, ships, and equipment keep the ports running. Truck activity is covered in the companion dashboard.

  2. 2

    Air Pollution Patterns

    What monitors near the ports measured: fine particles (PM2.5) and black carbon.

  3. 3

    Time & Location

    How measurements change by month, by year, by hour of day, and from one monitoring site to another.

  4. 4

    Community Relevance

    What these patterns may mean for neighborhoods near the ports, without assuming a cause.

 

Key Concepts

Everything on this dashboard builds on these four ideas.

  1. 1

    PM2.5

    Fine particles in the air, small enough to be inhaled deep into the lungs. Measured in micrograms per cubic meter (µg/m³).

  2. 2

    Black Carbon

    A sooty pollutant produced by combustion, commonly associated with sources like diesel truck and equipment engines.

  3. 3

    PM2.5 Exceedance

    A day (or period) when measured PM2.5 rises above the health-based benchmark used in this analysis.

  4. 4

    Diurnal Profile

    How a pollutant's level rises and falls over the 24 hours of a typical day.

PM2.5 & Black Carbon: Multi-Year Comparison

How did monthly PM2.5 and black carbon levels change from year to year and did all four sites see the same patterns?

Each small chart shows one monitoring site. Each colored line is one year of monthly averages, so higher points mean more pollution that month.

Read the full chart guide, key findings, and data caveats

What does this page show?

POLA runs four monitoring sites instead of POLB's two, so each pollutant below is shown as a 2×2 grid of site panels rather than one combined line. Each panel plots the monthly average concentration for every year, 2019 through 2025. It is broken out by site since POLA's four locations capture very different things (two are community-facing sites, one sits closest to port source activity, and one is a coastal background reference point).

  • Each colored line is one year. Higher points mean more pollution that month.
  • Use the toggle bar (stays fixed at the top) to show/hide a year across all eight panels at once.
  • Hover over any point for the exact monthly average.
Why this matters for the community: Comparing panels side by side shows whether a bad month is a regional event (shows up at all four sites) or a local one (shows up mainly at the site closest to port operations). This is exactly the distinction that matters for figuring out whether the port specifically is driving a given spike.
Data caveats to know before reading this chart:
  • Black carbon was only measured at the Source-Dominated site in 2019–2020; the other three sites didn't start BC monitoring until 2021, and Coastal Boundary's BC coverage in 2021 is partial.
  • Coastal Boundary's PM2.5 data is very sparse from 2020–2022 (as low as 0% in 2021) and only becomes reliably complete from 2023 onward. Treat early Coastal Boundary PM2.5 as mostly missing, not "clean."
  • Sharp single-day spikes on January 1st and July 4th each year (in the hundreds of µg/m³ for PM2.5) line up with fireworks holidays, not port activity. This is a well-documented nationwide pattern, not a data error.
  • A cluster of unusually high black carbon readings at Coastal Boundary in late May 2025 (20–89.5 µg/m³, versus ~16.5 µg/m³ max everywhere else in the entire dataset) has been kept in the data as requested, but most likely reflects an instrument issue rather than a real air quality event. Treat that specific week at that site with caution.

Hover over (or tap) any point for the exact monthly average. Use the year buttons to show or hide a year across all panels at once.

What this shows

Putting the four sites side by side shows whether a high month appeared at every site or mainly at one. Two sites are community locations, one sits closest to port source activity, and one is a coastal background reference point.

Lining up the years makes it easier to see which months looked typical and which stood out.

Why it matters

Separating area-wide conditions, like wildfire smoke, from patterns seen mainly at the site closest to port activity gives useful context about what nearby communities may be breathing. It does not, on its own, identify what caused any single high month.

Data context

These measurements describe pollution patterns at monitoring locations. They should not be interpreted as direct measures of individual health risk.

  • Black carbon was measured at the Source-Dominated site from 2019; the other three sites began in 2021 (Coastal Boundary's 2021 coverage is partial). Earlier years appear blank because nothing was measured.
  • Coastal Boundary PM2.5 is very sparse from 2020 to 2022.
  • Sharp spikes on January 1 and July 4 line up with fireworks holidays, not port activity.
  • The dashed line marks the EPA annual PM2.5 standard (9.0 µg/m³) as a flat reference.

Source: Port of Los Angeles Air Monitoring Data: Wilmington, San Pedro, Source-Dominated, and Coastal Boundary Sites
Period: 2019–2025, Monthly Averages

PM2.5 Exceedance Timeline

How many days did daily PM2.5 rise above the EPA's 24-hour limit of 35 µg/m³ and at which sites?

Bar charts count the days each year that a site's daily average was above the limit. Further down, daily timelines mark each of those days with a red dot.

Read the full chart guide, key findings, and data caveats

How to read this page

This page has two parts. First, a simple bar chart per site showing how many days each year crossed 35 µg/m³, the U.S. EPA's 24-hour PM2.5 health standard. Taller bars mean more unhealthy days that year. Second, there is also a detailed daily chart per site provided with the limit drawn as a dashed red line and every day that crossed it marked with a red dot.

  • Bar charts (below): show overall severity and trend at a glance. There is no line-chart reading required to get the headline number.
  • Daily timelines (further down): provide day-level detail to show exactly which days exceeded the limit, and by how much.
  • Both are broken out by site because POLA's four locations capture very different things: two are community-facing sites, one sits closest to port source activity, and one is a coastal background reference point.
Why this matters for the community: Wilmington, the community site closest to port and refinery activity has had more exceedance days than any other site in every year with meaningful data. That's a concrete, countable difference in how often the air was officially unhealthy for the people living there compared to the other three locations.
Data caveats to know before reading this chart:
  • Coastal Boundary has very little usable PM2.5 data before 2023 (see the multi-year comparison page). Its low exceedance count in early years likely reflects missing data, not clean air, and shouldn't be read as "Coastal Boundary was fine" for those years.
  • The dramatic single-hour fireworks spikes on January 1st and July 4th (in the hundreds of µg/m³) mostly do not show up as exceedance days here, because this chart uses the daily average (matching the EPA's 24-hour standard) and a one- or two-hour spike gets diluted across the other 22–23 normal hours in that day.
  • The worst days across every site cluster in September 2020, during major Southern California wildfires which is not a port-activity event.
Loading interactive chart…

Hover over (or tap) any bar or point for exact values.

What this shows

Wilmington had the most days above the limit (28), followed by Source-Dominated (16) and San Pedro (12). Coastal Boundary had 2, but it has large gaps in its data, so that count says little about its air.

The highest readings at every site cluster in September 2020, during major Southern California wildfires.

Why it matters

Counting days above a federal limit is a concrete way to compare sites and years, and to tell routine conditions from unusual events such as the September 2020 wildfires. It describes what the monitors recorded, not what any one person experienced.

Data context

These measurements describe pollution patterns at monitoring locations. They should not be interpreted as direct measures of individual health risk.

  • Coastal Boundary has very little usable PM2.5 data before 2023, so its low counts likely reflect missing data, not clean air.
  • Brief fireworks spikes on January 1 and July 4 mostly don't appear here: this chart uses daily averages (matching the 24-hour standard), which dilute a one- or two-hour spike.
  • Shaded bands on the daily timelines mark stretches with no data collected, not zero pollution.
  • The blue dashed line (9.0 µg/m³) is the EPA annual standard, shown as a flat reference. A single day above it is not a violation.

Source: Port of Los Angeles Air Monitoring Data — Four Monitoring Sites
Period: 2019–2025, Daily Averages

PM2.5 & Black Carbon: Multi-Year Comparison

How did PM2.5 and black carbon change from month to month and how does each month compare with the same month in other years?

Each small chart shows one monitoring site. Each colored line is one year of monthly averages, so higher points mean more pollution that month.

Read the full chart guide and key findings

What does this chart show?

This chart plots the average monthly concentration for each year: 2019, 2020, 2021, 2022, and 2023, as separate lines on the same graph. Each point on a line represents how much pollution was in the air during that calendar month in that year. Viewing all five years together makes it possible to see not just how polluted the air was in any given month, but how that level compares to the same month in prior years.

  • Each colored line represents one year. Higher points mean more pollution in the air that month.
  • Where lines converge, pollution levels were similar across years for that month, suggesting a normal seasonal pattern rather than something unusual.
  • Where a line spikes above the others, something out of the ordinary happened that month.
  • Use the toggle buttons to show or hide individual years for a cleaner comparison.
  • Hover over any point to see the exact monthly average for each year.
Why this matters for the community: The gap between the lowest month (March 2020 — 7.06 µg/m³) and the highest month (September 2020 — 24.99 µg/m³) is more than a 3x difference in PM2.5 levels. For people living and working near the port, that difference is the gap between a normal air quality day and a day where sensitive groups like children, older adults, people with asthma, are advised to limit outdoor activity.
Loading interactive chart…

Hover over (or tap) any point for the exact monthly average. Use the year buttons to show or hide individual years.

What this shows

Monthly PM2.5 averages ranged from 7.06 µg/m³ (March 2020) to 24.99 µg/m³ (September 2020, during wildfire smoke). Black carbon ranged from 0.32 µg/m³ (May 2019) to 2.26 µg/m³ (December 2020).

Where the lines sit close together, that month looked similar across years. Where one line rises above the others, that month stood out.

Why it matters

Comparing the same month across years helps separate normal seasonal patterns from unusual months, such as the wildfire smoke of September 2020. Black carbon is commonly associated with diesel engines and other combustion, so its pattern is a useful companion to PM2.5.

Data context

These measurements describe pollution patterns at monitoring locations. They should not be interpreted as direct measures of individual health risk.

  • 2023 covers January through March only.
  • The dashed line marks the EPA annual PM2.5 standard (9.0 µg/m³) as a flat reference for individual months.

Source: Port of Long Beach Air Monitoring Data
Period: January 2019 – March 2023, Monthly Averages

PM2.5 Exceedance Timeline

How often did daily PM2.5 near the Port of Long Beach rise above the EPA's 24-hour limit and how does a typical year compare with the annual guideline?

One line shows the daily average PM2.5 from January 2019 to March 2023. Dashed lines mark the EPA's 24-hour limit (35 µg/m³) and annual standard (9.0 µg/m³); red dots mark days above the 24-hour limit. A bar chart below counts those days by year.

Read the full chart guide and key findings

What does this chart show?

This chart plots the daily average PM2.5 concentration for every day in the dataset as a single continuous line. The dashed red line marks 35 µg/m³, the U.S. EPA's National Ambient Air Quality Standard (NAAQS) for 24-hour PM2.5 exposure which is the federal health-based limit no area is supposed to exceed. Any day where the line rises above that threshold is marked with a red dot.

  • The orange line is the day-by-day PM2.5 average. Higher points mean more pollution in the air that day.
  • The dashed red line is the health-based limit set by the EPA, not an arbitrary cutoff.
  • Red dots mark the specific days that crossed that limit. These are the days air quality was officially unhealthy by federal standards.
  • Hover over any point to see the exact date and concentration.
Why this matters for the community: Out of 1,549 days with usable data, only 14 days crossed the federal health limit and 10 of those 14 fell within a single month (September 2020), during major Southern California wildfires. That's useful context: it means routine, day-to-day port-area air quality rarely crosses this federal limit on its own but when it does, it tends to happen in short, intense clusters worth flagging individually, not as a slow year-round decline.
How POLB measures against both standards: Against the 24-hour limit, POLB stays under it the vast majority of the time. Only 0.9% of days on record crossed it, and almost entirely during one wildfire event rather than routine operations. Against the annual standard, the picture is different: every year in this dataset (2019–2023) averaged above 9.0 µg/m³, ranging from 11.25 to 14.64 µg/m³. In other words, POLB's air rarely has acutely dangerous single days, but its typical year-round baseline sits consistently above the EPA's health-based annual benchmark.
Loading interactive chart…

Hover over (or tap) any point for the exact date and concentration.

What this shows

Only 14 of 1,549 days with data (0.9%) went above the 24-hour limit, and 10 of those were in September 2020, during major Southern California wildfires.

Yearly averages tell a different story: every year from 2019 to 2023 averaged above 9.0 µg/m³, ranging from 11.25 to 14.64 µg/m³.

Why it matters

The same data can look different depending on the yardstick. Days above the daily limit were rare outside a wildfire period, while typical yearly levels sat above the annual benchmark. Looking at both gives a fuller picture of air quality near the port.

Data context

These measurements describe pollution patterns at monitoring locations. They should not be interpreted as direct measures of individual health risk.

  • The annual comparison uses simple year-by-year averages of this dataset.
  • A single day above 9.0 µg/m³ is not a violation. That standard applies to the annual average.
  • 2023 covers January through March only.

Source: Port of Long Beach Air Monitoring Data
Period: January 2019 – March 2023, Daily Averages

Black Carbon by Hour of Day

What does a typical day look like for black carbon, hour by hour and does it differ between two sites?

Each line shows the average black carbon level at each hour of the day, January 2019 to March 2023. Inner is a site closer to terminal and yard operations; Outer is farther away.

Read the full chart guide and key findings

What does this chart show?

This chart averages every hourly Black Carbon (BC) reading in the dataset into a single 24-point profile per site: what does a typical hour of the day look like, on average, at each monitor? There is over 33,000 hours at each site across four-plus years. Because BC is a true 1-hour average pollutant (unlike PM2.5, which is reported here as a smoothed 24-hour rolling average), it's the only pollutant in this dataset that can reveal a genuine hour-by-hour pattern.

  • The orange line is the Inner site which is closer to terminal and yard operations.
  • The blue line is the Outer site which is farther from active terminal operations.
  • Both sites peak sharply in the early morning, then fall through midday to an afternoon low, and climb again into the evening. This is a pattern consistent with diesel truck and drayage activity ramping up at the start of the operating day.
  • The gap between the lines is largest during the morning peak and narrowest overnight, meaning the Inner site's excess BC is concentrated in specific operational hours, not spread evenly across the day.
Key finding: BC at the Inner site peaks at 7:00 AM (1.62 µg/m³), about 42% higher than the Outer site at that same hour (1.14 µg/m³). Both sites hit their lowest point in the mid-to-late afternoon, around 4–5 PM, before climbing again toward midnight. The shape and timing of this pattern point to morning drayage and terminal-gate activity as a major driver of the localized BC gradient between the two sites.
Loading interactive chart…

Hover over (or tap) any hour to compare the two sites.

What this shows

Both sites peak in the early morning, dip to a low in the mid-to-late afternoon (around 4–5 PM), and climb again toward midnight.

At 7 AM the Inner site averaged 1.62 µg/m³ which is about 42% higher than the Outer site at that hour (1.14 µg/m³). The gap between the two sites is largest in the early morning.

Why it matters

Knowing when levels tend to be highest shows which times of day nearby air is most affected. The morning peak is consistent with the start of the busy operating day at the port, but a chart of averages cannot confirm what causes it.

Data context

These measurements describe pollution patterns at monitoring locations. They should not be interpreted as direct measures of individual health risk.

  • Each point is the average of all hourly readings at that hour of the day. There is roughly 1,300–1,400 readings per hour, per site.
  • Black carbon is measured as a true hourly average. PM2.5 is not shown because it is reported as a 24-hour rolling average and does not vary meaningfully by hour.

Source: Port of Long Beach Air Monitoring Data: Inner and Outer sites
Period: January 2019 – March 2023, Hourly Averages
